query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled carbon doping during synthesis will improve the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys by promoting local atomic disorder that retards crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloy prepared under rapid cooling conditions that yield an amorphous phase.
generation.intervention: Controlled incorporation of carbon during synthesis (e.g., via a carbon‐rich precursor or an organic solvent environment) to introduce active carbon species into the melt.
generation.conditions: Rapid quenching conditions where carbon can be uniformly incorporated at low concentrations; proper optimization is required to avoid excessive carbon that could lead to carbide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of carbon‐enriched interfacial or interstitial regions that increase local disorder.
generation.mechanism: Carbon doping increases local configurational entropy and retards atomic mobility, thereby suppressing crystalline nucleation and growth during solidification.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped samples, the carbon‐doped alloy is expected to exhibit a lower critical cooling rate, a larger critical casting diameter, and an increased glass transition temperature with delayed crystallization onset.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys processed under identical rapid cooling conditions without carbon doping.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only when the carbon concentration is within an optimal range; deviations from this range (either too high or too low) may lead to unwanted carbide formation or no improvement in amorphous stability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise carbon concentration for optimal performance and the quantitative extent of the improvement remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy samples under identical rapid quenching conditions. One set will be doped with a controlled amount of carbon through a carbon‐rich precursor or by processing in an organic liquid, and the other set will serve as the control without carbon doping.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the glass transition temperature and crystallization onset
X‐ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the amorphous structure and detect any crystalline or carbide phases
Measurement of the critical casting diameter to evaluate glass‐forming ability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon‐doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements in glass‐forming ability (e.g., no increase in critical casting diameter, glass transition temperature, or delayed crystallization onset) or if detrimental carbide formation is observed compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

An increase in entropy leads to a reduction of the Gibbs free energy for the amorphous phase, thereby favoring its formation over a crystalline phase. This principle underscores the preferential formation of the amorphous state in materials with high configurational entropy, which correlates with a greater glass-forming ability. The level of heterogeneity in atomic sizes and bonding characteristics among multiple elements serves to disrupt the crystal nucleation process and slow down grain growth, further favoring the development of amorphous structures over crystalline structures. Therefore, configuration entropy is pivotal in predicting the glass-forming ability of AMAs and ensuring their stability as noncrystalline solids.

This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of a microalloying element that preferentially interacts with phosphorus will improve both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus‐containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy in its as-mixed/liquid state prior to rapid quenching.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a low concentration of a carefully selected microalloying element (without presupposing its specific chemical class) that has a high chemical affinity for phosphorus.
drafts.conditions: Samples processed under identical rapid quenching conditions; the intervention is expected to work in compositions where phosphorus is a key component for the amorphous phase and where the microalloying element does not form unwanted secondary phases.
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced local atomic ordering through preferential bonding between phosphorus and the microalloying element, leading to greater heterogeneity that impedes crystalline nucleation.
drafts.mechanism: The microalloying element forms strong bonds with phosphorus, thereby stabilizing local amorphous configurations and elevating the energy barrier for crystallization, which increases both the critical cooling rate for glass formation and the onset temperature for crystallization.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should display a higher resistance to crystallization, evident as an increased onset temperature for crystallization and/or a reduced critical cooling rate for glass formation relative to an otherwise comparable baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy prepared and rapidly quenched under identical conditions but without the microalloying element.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is contingent on the proper selection and optimal concentration of the microalloying element; if the added element is not well-matched with the alloy’s chemistry or is used in too high a concentration, it might instead form separate phases or have no beneficial effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples with identical base compositions. Introduce the microalloying element at a designated low concentration into one set (intervention) while keeping the other set as the control. Process both sets under identical rapid-quenching conditions and subsequently evaluate their thermal responses via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and phase analysis using X-ray diffraction.
measurements: Critical cooling rate for glass formation
Onset temperature of crystallization from DSC
Thermal stability (e.g., glass transition and crystallization temperature shifts)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microalloyed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in either the critical cooling rate required for glass formation or in the onset temperature for crystallization (i.e., if the measured thermal stability metrics are equivalent to or worse than those of the control samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Elevated external pressure applied during the melt-quenching process enhances the glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy melt prepared under standard composition conditions.
drafts.intervention: Melt-quenching under controlled, elevated pressure (in an inert atmosphere) instead of conventional ambient pressure processing.
drafts.conditions: This intervention should be applied during quenching from the melt; it is expected to be effective only when the alloy’s composition (especially the phosphorus content) and melt viscosity are within a range that allows pressure to significantly reduce atomic mobility. It may not work if dramatic changes in composition result in different atomic interactions.
drafts.structural_mediator: A reduction in free volume and an increase in the homogeneity of atomic packing in the amorphous state, which together raise the energy barriers for nucleation of crystalline phases.
drafts.mechanism: Elevated external pressure during cooling is expected to increase the melt viscosity and promote a denser, more uniform atomic arrangement. This suppressed mobility and enhanced atomic packing delay the kinetics of crystallization, thereby improving both the critical cooling rate required for glass formation and the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous phase.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to samples processed at ambient pressure, high-pressure quenched alloys will exhibit a lower (i.e., more favorable) critical cooling rate for glass formation and a higher onset temperature for crystallization as detected by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).
drafts.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys produced by conventional melt-quenching at ambient pressure.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is expected only within a specific window of alloy compositions and processing conditions where melt viscosity and phosphorus content do not overwhelm the pressure effect. Results may differ if the alloy contains additional elements that alter the atomic mobility in unexpected ways.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy melts with the same composition. Process one set using conventional ambient pressure melt-quenching and the other set by applying a controlled elevated external pressure during the melt-quenching process. Characterize both sets using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the onset temperature for crystallization and by measuring the critical cooling rate (e.g., via X-ray diffraction analysis to confirm amorphous structure).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm phase structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-pressure melt-quenched samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature and do not require a lower critical cooling rate to achieve an amorphous state compared to the ambient pressure samples, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of carbon during processing (i.e., carbon doping) will improve the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous phase in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys synthesized under rapid quenching conditions, where the amorphous phase is formed but may have limited thermal stability.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate controlled carbon doping during synthesis (for example, by using an organic liquid environment during laser ablation or by adding a carbon-rich precursor) to deliver active carbon species into the melt.
drafts.conditions: Under rapid cooling conditions (e.g., nanosecond laser ablation or high-rate quenching) where carbon has the opportunity to diffuse minimally into forming particles; the intervention is expected to be effective if carbon incorporation can occur without forming excessive carbide precipitates.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of thin carbon-enriched layers or carbon-modified interfacial regions that inhibit atomic rearrangement into crystalline phases and stabilize the disordered (amorphous) structure.
drafts.mechanism: Carbon doping increases local structural disorder and lowers atomic mobility, thereby enhancing configurational entropy and acting as a kinetic barrier to crystallization. This suppression of nucleation and growth increases the ability of the alloy to remain amorphous and thermally stable.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloys will exhibit a lower critical cooling rate, a larger attainable amorphous casting diameter (Dmax), and higher glass transition temperatures (Tg) plus a delayed onset of crystallization relative to comparable alloys without carbon doping.
drafts.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed under similarly rapid cooling conditions without controlled carbon doping.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent on optimizing the carbon concentration; excessive carbon might lead to carbide formation or other deleterious secondary phases, and insufficient carbon incorporation may not yield a measurable improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples using the same rapid quenching method. One set will be doped with a controlled amount of carbon (using an organic liquid or carbon-rich precursor) while the other set, serving as the control, will be processed without carbon doping. Use identical cooling rates and processing conditions for both sets.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) and exothermic crystallization onset.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the degree of amorphization and detect any crystalline phases or carbide precipitates.
Measurement of the critical casting diameter (Dmax) for fully amorphous rods or plates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in glass-forming ability (i.e., exhibit no higher Tg, larger Dmax, or more suppressed crystallization exotherms) compared to the control samples processed without carbon, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of carbon into phosphorus‐containing high-entropy alloys will improve both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous phase.
drafts.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) processed without additional carbon doping.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a controlled level of carbon (via either adding a suitable carbon precursor during alloy synthesis or carbonizing the melt) so that carbon is uniformly distributed in the alloy.
drafts.conditions: The beneficial effect should manifest when the alloy is rapidly cooled (e.g., via melt spinning) under conditions that prevent carbon segregation; if carbon concentration exceeds its solubility or leads to carbide formation, the intervention may not work.
drafts.structural_mediator: The introduction of carbon is expected to form a carbon-enriched interfacial layer or interstitial sites that increase local disorder and inhibit the nucleation of crystalline phases.
drafts.mechanism: Carbon atoms, when uniformly incorporated, increase atomic-level disorder and lower the Gibbs free energy of the amorphous state by retarding crystalline nucleation, thus improving both the glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to an otherwise identical alloy without carbon, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit a larger critical casting diameter (indicating enhanced glass-forming ability) and a higher and more stable glass transition temperature (Tg) as measured by thermal analysis.
drafts.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy processed under identical conditions but without any deliberate carbon addition.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be beneficial only within an optimal carbon concentration window. Exceeding this limit may lead to carbide precipitation or phase separation, which would negate the improvement in amorphous stability.

Ensure identical processing conditions (e.g., cooling rates, sample geometry).
measurements: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) and crystallization exotherms
Measurement of critical casting diameter (Dmax) to assess glass-forming ability
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to examine amorphous versus crystalline phase content
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Dmax or higher and more stable Tg relative to the control alloy, or if evidence of detrimental carbide formation is observed that compromises the amorphous microstructure, then the hypothesis is falsified.
